title: Unit 2: Earth’s Place within the Cosmos
sub: Reading: pages 22–38  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

questions.stem: When astronomers observe redshift in the light coming from a distant galaxy, they know that
choices: the galaxy is moving away from Earth
the galaxy contains a black hole
the galaxy is made mostly of hydrogen
questions.why: p. 24 — redshift occurs when the light source moves away from the observer, or when the space between them stretches. Because all galaxies show redshift, the universe must be expanding.

choices: the universe will eventually stop expanding and contract
light always travels at a constant speed
all galaxies are roughly the same distance apart
the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us
questions.why: p. 24 — Hubble combined distance measurements with redshift data and found this relationship, which leads to the hypothesis that the universe is expanding.

questions.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, the universe began about
questions.why: p. 25 — 4.6 billion years is the age of the solar system, not the universe. 380,000 years is how long after the Big Bang the first neutral atoms formed.

questions.stem: What is the energy source for all stars?
questions.why: p. 33 — in the core of a star, pressure is great enough that two hydrogen atoms fuse to become a helium atom.

questions.stem: A group of tens to hundreds of thousands of mostly reddish stars, held tightly together by gravity in a definite spherical shape, is a
questions.why: p. 29 — open clusters, by contrast, hold up to a few thousand young bluish stars loosely, and still contain glowing gas and dust.

questions.stem: Earth sits about how far from the center of the Milky Way Galaxy?
questions.why: p. 32 — a little more than halfway out from the center to the edge. The disk itself is about 100,000 light-years across.

questions.stem: Elliptical galaxies appear reddish to yellowish because they contain mostly old stars.
questions.why: p. 30 — most elliptical galaxies also contain very little gas and dust, because it has already formed into stars.

questions.stem: The Milky Way is classified as an irregular galaxy.
questions.why: The Milky Way is a typical spiral galaxy, with a disk, a central bulge, and spiral arms. (p. 31)

questions.stem: Astronomers use two different terms: dark matter and dark energy. Briefly explain what each one is used to account for.
questions.answer: Dark matter accounts for missing mass; dark energy accounts for the accelerating expansion of the universe.
questions.rubric: 1.5 pts each. Dark matter: there is far too little visible matter to make up the roughly 27% of the universe that observations require, so dark matter is the name for that unseen mass. Scientists are more certain what it is not — not stars and planets, not baryonic clouds, not antimatter, not galaxy-sized black holes. Dark energy: a hypothetical form of energy, possibly as much as 72% of the universe’s total energy content, proposed to explain why the rate of expansion is increasing rather than slowing. (pp. 26–28)

questions.stem: Describe what happens to a typical star like our Sun once it has burned up all of the helium in its core.
questions.answer: Fusion stops completely, and gravitational collapse shrinks the star’s core into a white dwarf.
questions.rubric: 1 pt fusion stops; 1 pt gravitational collapse of the core; 1 pt the result is a white dwarf — a white, glowing object about the size of Earth — which eventually fades out. Award credit if the student also describes the earlier red giant stage (outer layers grow outward and cool, turning the star red). Do not give credit for supernova, neutron star, or black hole — those require a much more massive star. (p. 36)
